16 measures made the Data Breach a foreseeable, and even likely, consequence of its negligence.

 8          9.      Through this lawsuit, Plaintiff seeks to hold Defendant responsible for the injuries it

10 and to seek injunctive relief to ensure the implementation of security measures to protect the Private

11 Information that remains in Defendant’s possession.

12          10.     The exposure of one’s Private Information to cybercriminals is a bell that cannot be un-
13 rung. Before this Data Breach, Plaintiff’s and the Class’s Private Information was exactly that—

14 private. Not anymore. Now, their Private Information is forever exposed and unsecure.

15                                      JURISDICTION AND VENUE

16          11.     The Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action under the Class Action

17 Fairness Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2). The amount in controversy exceeds $5 million, exclusive of

18 interest and costs. Upon information and belief, the number of Class Members exceeds 100, many of

19 whom have different citizenship from Defendant. Thus, minimal diversity exists under 28 U.S.C. §

20 1332(d)(2)(A).

21          12.     The Court has general personal jurisdiction over Defendant because Defendant’s

22 headquarters and principal place of business is located in this District.

23          13.     Venue is proper in this Court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391, because it is the District

24 within which Defendant has the most significant contacts.

25                                                  PARTIES

26          14.     Plaintiff is, and at all relevant times has been, a resident and citizen of California, where

27 she intends to remain.

28          15.     Defendant is a California corporation with its headquarters and principal place of

 2                                      FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

 3       A. The Data Breach

 4          16.      As a condition of receiving a healthcare plan or services, Plaintiff and Class Members

 5 were required to provide Defendant with their sensitive and confidential Private Information, including

 6 their names, mailing addresses, emails, telephone numbers, dates of birth, driver’s licenses, medical

 7 diagnosis or conditions, and health insurance information.

 8          17.    Defendant did not use reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the
 9 nature of the sensitive information it was maintaining for Plaintiff and Class Members, such as

10 encrypting the information or deleting it when it is no longer needed, causing the exposure of Private

11 Information.

12          18.    As evidenced by the Data Breach, the Private Information contained in Defendant’s
13 network and was not encrypted. Had the information been properly encrypted, the data thieves would

14 have exfiltrated only unintelligible data.

15       B. The Value of Private Information
16          19.    In April 2020, ZDNet reported in an article titled “Ransomware mentioned in 1,000+
17 SEC filings over the past year”, that “[r]ansomware gangs are now ferociously aggressive in their

18 pursuit of big companies. They breach networks, use specialized tools to maximize damage, leak

19 corporate information on dark web portals, and even tip journalists to generate negative news for

20 complaints as revenge against those who refuse to pay.” 7

21          20.    In September 2020, the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security

22 Agency published online a “Ransomware Guide” advising that “[m]alicious actors have adjusted their

23 ransomware tactics over time to include pressuring victims for payment by threatening to release

24 stolen data if they refuse to pay and publicly naming and shaming victims as secondary forms of

25 extortion.” 8

26          21.    Stolen Private Information is often trafficked on the dark web, as is the case here. Law

 4        C. Defendant Failed to Comply with Regulatory Requirements and Standards.

 5           32.   Federal and state regulators have established security standards and issued

 6 recommendations to temper data breaches and the resulting harm to consumers and employees. There

 7 are a number of state and federal laws, requirements, and industry standards governing the protection

 8 of Private Information.
 9           33.   For example, at least 24 states have enacted laws addressing data security practices that
10 require businesses that own, license, or maintain Private Information about a resident of that state to

11 implement and maintain “reasonable security procedures and practices” and to protect Private

12 Information from unauthorized access.

13           34.   Additionally, cybersecurity firms have promulgated a series of best practices that at a
14 minimum should be implemented by sector participants including, but not limited to: installing

15 appropriate malware detection software; monitoring and limiting network ports; protecting web

16 browsers and email management systems; setting up network systems such as firewalls, switches, and

17 routers; monitoring and protecting of physical security systems; protecting against any possible

18 communication system; and training staff regarding critical points. 17

19           35.   The FTC has issued several guides for businesses, highlighting the importance of

20 reasonable data security practices. According to the FTC, the need for data security should be

21 considered for all business decision-making. 18

22           36.   Under the FTC’s 2016 Protecting Personal Information: Guide for Business

23 publication, the FTC notes that businesses should safeguard the personal customer information they

24 retain; properly dispose of unnecessary personal information; encrypt information stored on computer

 3          37.    The guidelines also suggest that businesses use an intrusion detection system to expose

 4 a breach as soon as it happens, monitor all incoming traffic for activity indicating someone is trying

 5 to hack the system, watch for large amounts of data being siphoned from the system, and have a

 6 response plan in the event of a breach.

 7          38.    The FTC advises companies to not keep information for periods of time longer than

 8 needed to authorize a transaction, restrict access to private information, mandate complex passwords
 9 to be used on networks, utilize industry-standard methods for security, monitor for suspicious activity

10 on the network, and verify that third-party service providers have implemented reasonable security

11 measures. 20

12          39.    The FTC has brought enforcement actions against companies for failing to adequately

13 and reasonably protect consumer data, treating the failure to do so as an unfair act or practice barred

14 by Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act (“FTCA”), 15 U.S.C. § 45. Orders originating from

15 these actions further elucidate the measures businesses must take to satisfy their data security

16 obligations.

17          40.    Defendant’s failure to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect against

18 unauthorized access to confidential consumer data constitutes an unfair act or practice prohibited by

19 Section 5 of the FTCA, 15 U.S.C. § 45.

20          41.    Defendant’s failure to verify that it had implemented reasonable security measures

21 constitutes an unfair act or practice prohibited by Section 5 of the FTCA, 15 U.S.C. § 45.

22          42.    Furthermore, Defendant is required to comply with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, 45 C.F.R.

25 Health Information”), 45 C.F.R. Part 160 and Part 164, Subparts A and C. The Privacy Rule and the

26 Security Rule set nationwide standards for protecting health information, including health information
